[h1]"We all make Choices, But in the End our choices make us."[/h1]

It's hard to write about a game as classic as [b]Bioshock[/b]. I remember renting this game for xbox 360 from a Blockbuster that I worked at in 2008. I didn't know what it was, but I had just come off one of the best gaming experiences of my life in Mass Effect and wanted something new. [i]Different. Unique.[/i] Bioshock promised that and delivered back then. Bioshock: Remastered managed to re-deliver on that original promise of being a shooter unlike any other. In a year unlike any other, (2020) and whose implications for our world are equally as terrifying as the game's masked lunatic drug addicts with magic powers and little girls that drain blood from murder victims.

I decided to play Bioshock again for one reason. I needed something [i]different.[/i] I had been playing a lot of souls like, horror, rpg, platforming, puzzle, adventure, shooter... basically every genre one can imagine exists in 2020 while stuck at home. Bioshock: Remastered was the only thing in my massive library of backlogged games that stuck out as something different from all the other things. Like I said: "It Delivered" again. It broke me out of a rut and got me interested in revisiting old favorites again, now that it had been a decade or more since I last thought about them.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You begin Bioshock as a man named Jack on an unknown flight off to some mysterious destination for some unfamiliar reason. As you light up your smoke (it is 1960 after all, did I mention that?) and look to open a gift given to you by your parents... the plane ignites and crashes into the ocean. The sole survivor, you find a light house in the middle of the ocean that is more than it seems. This is RAPTURE! An underwater city built by a man named Andrew Ryan. Rapture was a haven for Science, Industry and Art undisturbed by intervention from governments, religion, or other social agencies. Believing real progress couldn't be made while under the gaze of society and it's laws and morals. As Ryan says: 

[h1]"It wasn't impossible to build a city under the ocean, it was impossible to build Rapture anywhere else!"[/h1]

Arriving in the city you quickly realize things are not as amazing and as great as they seem from the introduction played on the projector as you are lowered into the dark ocean. Met immediately by blood and violence you set off into Rapture taking instruction from a man named Atlas looking for his family and you are now his only hope. Now would you kindly find a crowbar or something and help him out? You do. You find out Rapture has been in a massive and sharp decline. A class war has broken out and the poor  (construction workers who built the city, pretty much) have no jobs and are unable to fit in or afford a life among all the other perfect specimens of humanity. The best of the best that Rapture is made of. A new technology, known as Plasmids, have not only given people what basically equals Magic powers, but it has driven them insane and the entire city either lies dead, dying, or are the ones doing the killing. Known as Splicers, few left in Rapture are truly human anymore and this dark, deep, isoloated city at the bottom of the ocean has become a horror show. You are now a part of it. Along with several power mad, totally psychopathic, murder loving artists, scientists, and socialites.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Bioshock is a first person shooter before anything else. One of the first of it's kind to have such a unique atmosphere and RPG like mechanics. While the shooting isn't the best of the bunch, especially in 2020 when this has basically been perfected; the weapons, abilities, and all the other mechanics come together to form an immersive and satisfying FPS. Weapons are pretty standard by modern expectations. A pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, crossbow... but also some unique things like a research camera and chemical thrower, all very mechanical and steampunk. All weapons have several different ammo types you can find or craft, along with 3 upgrades each. Where bioshock gets interesting is with it's plasmids (spells). You have your fireball and electric blast powers (that will melt ice, set enemies on fire, or electrocute enemies standing in water) but you also have insect swarm, with bugs crawling around and beneath your skin on screen, and Telekenisis [i](to throw those pesky grenades right back at em!)[/i] among many others with many varying applications. You can buy and sell supplies at vending machines:

[h1]WELCOME TO THE CIRCUS OF VALUES![/h1]

that yell that at you as well as hack literally anything mechanical around for extra materials or discounts. And this game is pretty much steampunk, so almost everything is a machine. Hacking takes form of individual tunnel puzzles making you connect the flowing ooze from one end of a block to another by rearranging tiles to point the ooze in the correct direction. At first all of this seems a little unwieldy. Hacking takes you out of the gameplay time and space, switching weapons, ammo, powers, etc... isn't as easy or quick as it should be. I was quite frustrated for the first hour or so when I realized I was accidentally pumping my anti-personel rounds into a turret. Like most games, with a little bit of practice and persistence (and upgrades) I was hacking like a pro and flinging my powers and weapons around like I had been doing it my whole life.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
There were no noticeable bugs at all during my play through of Bioshock: remastered. I'm including this section because I have read quite a few reviews about constant crashing or other issues and I am happy to say I didn't have any of these. I experienced one crash during the game that cost me about 5 minutes of play time with about 13ish hours of playtime total. I played at 1080p with all options turned to max at a solid 60 fps or above the entire time with what I consider a mid tier gaming PC. If that's all you're looking for then you will probably be stoked and have no issues.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

[b]Overall Score: 9/10[/b]
[b]Why play?:[/b] Bioshock is considered a [i]"Must Play"[/i] video game by most of the industry and is considered to be one of the greatest video games of all time. A demonstration of video games as an art form. I agree with this.
[b]Why you shouldn't play?:[/b] If a visual overhaul isn't good enough to get you to play a 12 year old game. If you scare easy or have Thalassophobia. (Although my wife with Thalassophobia says Bioshock isn't bad in that regard.)

There really isn't much more to say. If you haven't played Bioshock yet then you're either just getting into these types of games, or actively decided not to play it for some reason. With a perfect blend of Horror, Science, Steampunk, Magic, Mystery, and of course [b]SHOOTING[/b]... with a story that is a must, if you believe video games are an art form, and with two sequels that are also really strong, you can't go wrong here with the upgraded visuals of the remastered version.

Bioshock Remastered is a fantastic game, and I recommend to everyone to play it! BUT it has a couple of annoying technical bugs and these can spoil the experience. I found solutions for these in different places on the internet so I thought I'd collect it to those who would just start playing with this game. 

The good news is that these bugs can be fixed before the game, at the beginning and after that personally I DID NOT EXPERIENCE ANY ERRORS OR BUGS DURING THE WHOLE GAME! The game looked beautiful, ran smoothly without any error or crashing! :)

My PC configuration is: 
Intel i5-8400, 16 GB RAM, NVIDIA 1060 6GB, Windows 10 Pro

So let's see the bugs and the solutions!

***********************************************************
Problem: Subtitle can't be set in the menu.

Solution:

1. Show hidden files in the folders of your Windows (if it's not already set):
https://www.technipages.com/show-hidden-files-windows
2. Find Bioshock.ini file
C:\Users\username\AppData\Roaming\BioshockHD\Bioshock\
3. Edit Bioshock.ini file
find DialogSubtitles=False (near at the bottom of the list):
and rewrite to DialogSubtitles=True
4. Save it
5. Restart the game and now you can set the Subtitle to ON/OFF in the menu

*************************************************************
Problem: Strangely you can set brightness only ONCE in the game. After that if you change in the menu, there will be no effect on the game and because the game default brightness setting is too dark it's not good. (they say this problem typically comes with win 10)

Solution: You have to switch OFF the Win 10 Fullscreen Optimizations for Bioshock

1. Find BioshockHD.exe file
It's in your Steam libary, at my PC it was in this folder:
steamapps\common\BioShock Remastered\Build\Final\
2. Right click on the BioshockHD.exe file and choose Properties
3. Click on the Compatibility tab and UNCHECK Disable fullscreen optimizations
4. Restart the game and after that you can set the Brightness 

******************************************************************
Problem: in the game at some parts of the screen there are vibrant black stripes.

Solution: in the menu set vsync to ON and the vibrant black stripes are gone

******************************************************************
Problem: in the menu you can set the game's audio, but these have no effect in the game (the voices were too quiet for me and other sounds were too loud)

Solution: 

1. Go to the Bioshock.ini file (see above) and you can find at the bottom of the list these: 
SFXVolume=100
MusicVolume=100
VoVolume=100
2. You can rewrite the values as you want and save the file. 
3. If you restart the game the sounds will be based on these settings.
*******************************************************************

I hope I helped some of you with these. :)

[h1]BioShock™ Remastered – Welcome Back to Rapture[/h1]
[b]Some games age gracefully, and then there’s BioShock, a masterpiece that doesn’t just age well, it evolves. The Remastered version gives a new coat of polish to one of the most iconic and atmospheric games ever made. Even after all these years, stepping into the underwater city of Rapture feels like discovering a forgotten world, one filled with beauty, madness, and philosophical questions that make you stare at your monitor long after the credits roll.[/b]

[h1]Welcome to Rapture – The City Beneath the Sea[/h1]
[b]It all begins with a plane crash and a descent into darkness, literally. You enter Rapture, an underwater utopia gone horribly wrong, built by the visionary (and slightly egomaniacal) Andrew Ryan. The moment those bronze doors open and the haunting theme plays, you realize this isn’t just a shooter, it’s an experience.
Every inch of Rapture tells a story. Cracked art-deco walls, leaking ceilings, eerie recordings of long-gone citizens, it’s environmental storytelling at its best. You can almost feel the weight of the ocean pressing down on this broken paradise, and yet… you can’t help but want to explore more.[/b]

[h1]Gameplay – When Guns Meet Genes[/h1]
[b]BioShock blends first-person shooting with plasmid powers, basically, you shoot lightning from your hands one second and blast enemies with a shotgun the next. The combat is creative, chaotic, and full of experimentation. Want to set a group of enemies on fire, then electrify the water they run through? You can. Want to turn a security bot against its master? Go right ahead.
The freedom of choice is what makes the gameplay so addictive. You’re constantly balancing resources, hacking machines, managing health, and deciding whether to save or harvest the Little Sisters (a moral choice that still hits hard today).
The Remastered version doesn’t change much about the gameplay, and honestly, it doesn’t need to. The original formula still holds up beautifully.[/b]

[h1]A Story That Still Sparks Debate[/h1]
[b]The writing in BioShock is nothing short of genius. The philosophy behind Rapture, freedom without morality, ambition without limits, is fascinating. Andrew Ryan’s speeches are chillingly relevant even today. And that plot twist... oh, that plot twist. If you’ve played it, you know what I’m talking about. If you haven’t, would you kindly experience it yourself?
It’s one of those rare games that make you question not only the world around you but your own role as a player. The way it breaks the fourth wall is nothing short of brilliant.[/b]

[h1]The Remaster – A Polished Dive[/h1]
[b]When the Remastered version first launched, it had its share of issues, crashes, bugs, and performance hiccups that made Rapture feel more like a sinking ship than an underwater city. Thankfully, those days are gone. After several patches, the game now runs smoothly and looks gorgeous.
Textures are sharper, lighting is richer, and the atmosphere feels even more immersive. It’s not a full-blown remake, but the improvements are enough to make a return trip worthwhile, especially for those who got it free with the original release.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]One of the best story-driven FPS experiences ever made
[*]Unique and unforgettable setting (an underwater city still unmatched in design)
[*]Excellent voice acting and haunting soundtrack
[*]Deep philosophical narrative with moral choices that actually matter
[*]Creative combat combining weapons and plasmid powers
[*]Remastered visuals make it even more atmospheric
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Occasional minor bugs and some dated animations
[*]Backtracking can feel repetitive in later sections
[*]AI can be a little too predictable at times
[/list]
[h1]Verdict:[/h1]
[b]BioShock Remastered is more than just a return to a classic, it’s a reminder of what makes gaming an art form. It’s a perfect blend of storytelling, gameplay, and atmosphere that few titles have managed to replicate even today.
When I first played it, the concept of an underwater city absolutely blew my mind, and even now, it still does. Rapture remains one of the most hauntingly beautiful locations in all of gaming history.
So if you’ve never descended into the depths of Rapture, it’s time to fix that. And if you have, well, there’s no harm in another dive. Just remember...

“A man chooses. A slave obeys.”

While I am marking this review as not recommended, my opinion is more "neutral".  Basically, the remaster is a hit and a miss for me. 

It does some things right:
-  updating resolution support
- Controller support
- Added content from console specific releases
- Trading cards and collectibles
- Directors commentary (cool, but could have just been added to OG release for free, didn’t need remaster)

It does many thing REALLY wrong:
- Removing the water reflective surfaces (makes everything look flat as hell, and pre-2003 graphics) 
- Removed Caustic Effects
- Changed the AI, now AI is a lot worse and lacks things the original had (like hanging on walls, and more advanced attack patterns/pathing. They are also Dumb now, you can light them on fire, and they run around until they die, and don’t seek out water sources to put themselves out like in the original. HUGE DOWNGRADE)
- Changed the audio system and samples. Its much worse than the original game. 
- Changing a lot of the aesthetics away from the original design
- Did not update a lot of textures properly, just upscalled the originals. (Very lazy job overall, community mods are a lot better)

Overall, I would recommend to only play it with mods, and only buy it on a good sale. The original is “better” if you get some community mods to add more modern support, but the remaster is more “user friendly” for people not familiar with modding and no knowledge of the originals design.

Bioshock is one of the most cult games of 2007, a year rich in excellent FPS.
Its score of 96 on Metacritic, the same as Half-Life and Half-Life 2, 
ranks it among the video game classics.
The game is close to perfection in many ways that I will discuss here.
Obviously, the Remastered version further improves the game in order to stay up to date. 

"Son, you're special, you were born to do great things." - Jack
1960. Somewhere above the sea. Jack, is on board a plane, a rather ordinary flight.
When suddenly, the plane suffers a technical breakdown and crashes into the sea...
Jack appears to be the only survivor of the flight, and although injured and disoriented, eventually reaches a nearby lighthouse... 

"I choose the impossible. I choose... Rapture." - Andrew Ryan
This lighthouse is actually the entrance to Rapture.
This utopian underwater city is the dream of Andrew Ryan, 
a rich megalomaniac businessman dreaming of another world.
Like a modern Atlantis, this city seems at the cutting edge of technology and is thought of as a paradise for good people.
The artistic direction is just sublime: 
Rapture is an ode to the fifties, revisited with steampunk style.
The shops, the advertisements, the music, everything is deliciously vintage.
The atmosphere is both warm and disturbing, as if you were lulled by a Lovecraft novel.

"A man chooses. A slave obeys." - Andrew Ryan
Obviously, reality is always different from propaganda.
In terms of paradise, Rapture is more of an underwater hell.
The rivalry between Andrew Ryan and his sworn enemy Frank Fontaine is more than harmful for Rapture...
The population serves either as slaves for Ryan or as Adam's reserves for Fontaine.
As a result, the population that has undergone scientific experiments is prey to paranoid and psychopathic delusions.
These unfortunate people are the Chrosomes. Their humanity gradually leaves their body, corrupted by Adam:
Mothers deploring the disappearance of their darling daughter, madmen of God proselytizing, fallen artists, etc...

"ADAM is a canvas of genetic modification… but Plasmids are the paint." - Dr Suchong
The main originality of the game is the system of Adam and Plasmids.
Tha Adam is a mysterious substance that allows you to modify people's DNA and give them powerful powers called Plasmids...
Let's say that Adam functions in Bioshock like Mana in a traditional RPG.
For example, you can throw lightning, fire, ice, attract objects using telekinesis, etc...
Plasmids can be upgraded to be even more powerful!

"I like getting Adam. It makes me special!" - Little Sisters
Adam's greatest source is found in the little sisters.
These little girls glean Adam from corpses.
They are escorted by the Big Daddies, genetically enhanced humans equipped with heavy armored suits.
They act as mini-bosses, armed with rivet guns and a large drill (that you can't use).
If you eliminate them, the little girls find themselves at your mercy...
Will you show humanity by saving these poor children from the evil that torments them?
Or will you shamelessly harvest them, in order to earn their precious powers?

"Don't be a slow poke, Mr. B. Angels don't wait for slow pokes." - Little Sisters
This is not a "Quake-Like" as they said at the time, but rather of an adventure game in subjective view.
Your character is quite slow and heavy, you can't run.
The game has fairly classic weaponry, offering for example a Revolver, a Grenade Launcher, a Crossbow, a Shotgun...
Combat becomes intense if there are many enemies.
You will find your enemies' weak point using the search camera.
The game is not always easy, and offers an interesting respawn system: the Vita-Chambers.
Rather than restarting where you saved last time, you respawn at these checkpoints,
but you don't lose your progress! Handy if you're struggling against a Big Daddy!
The game features a hacking system:
You can hack turrets and drones so that they are allies, the ending machines in order to have a better price, etc...

"Ain't life in Rapture grand?" - Bill McDonagh
You know it if you have read this far: Bioshock is indeed a masterpiece among FPS games.
Its atmosphere is exceptional, its scenario rich in twists and turns, the game is teeming with details and possibilities.
There are few games that will capture your feelings and make you reflect on your own humanity.
Bioshock has its place in the FPS pantheon.

Welcome to [u]BioShock Remastered[/u], where the magic of a classic is given a second life under a fresh coat of paint and a boost of light. BioShock is already a video game monument, but what does this remastered version offer us? A nostalgic trip to a slightly brighter Rapture? An even more immersive dive into this decaying utopia? Or just a nice Instagram filter on a dystopian world? Prepare yourself for an analysis where shadow and light duel. Is BioShock Remastered worth your attention? That's what we're going to see.

[b]Good points[/b]
[u]Careful graphic remaster:[/u] First thing that strikes you when playing BioShock Remastered is the visual improvement. We find sharper textures, redesigned lighting effects, and refined graphics that make Rapture even more striking. Deep, shimmering waters appear more alive, the details of Art Deco structures are even more striking, and reflections on glass and metal add immersive realism. Without reinventing the wheel, BioShock Remastered manages to give a fresh look to an already superb game.

[u]Even more oppressive atmosphere:[/u] Remastering also accentuates the sinister atmosphere of Rapture. Shadows are deeper, the crackling lights of neon add to the unease, and the revisited sound effects immerse players in a total immersion. Put on a headset, you can hear every drop of water falling, every whisper of Splicer in the dark corridors. The Big Daddies resonate in your ears with more power, making you hesitate before turning the next corner.

[u]More accessible version:[/u] Thanks to graphical adjustments and the improvement of certain mechanics, BioShock Remastered is more accessible for modern players. Those who missed out on the game in 2007 can now enjoy it in a more engaging and less dated form, without sacrificing the essence of the experience. In addition, this edition includes the DLC and offers bonus content such as concept art and developer commentary, which enriches the experience for newcomers and long-time fans alike.

[b]Bad points[/b]
[u]Persistent technical mimitations:[/u] While the game has undergone a visual update, the 2007 mechanics are still felt at times. Character animations can feel stiff, enemy AI is often predictable, and some bugs that were present in the original version are still strangely present. While this can be overlooked, it may frustrate modern players who expect a smooth, seamless experience.

[u]Aggravated combat repetition:[/u] BioShock has always suffered from repetitive gameplay, and the remastered version is no exception. The "explore-combat-resource gathering" cycle is repeated frequently, which can make some sections of the game feel a bit redundant. Sure, the atmosphere and story keep things interesting, but it can get repetitive, especially towards the end of the game.

[u]Wet Paint effect:[/u] For players who have already explored Rapture from top to bottom, BioShock Remastered can feel like they've seen it before. The changes, while significant, don't really add anything new to the game. Aside from the graphics layer, the remastered version doesn't bring any additional content or game mechanics. In short, it's more of a nice "restoration" than a real rediscovery for fans of the first day.

[u]Mixed technical performance:[/u] Ironically, despite the graphical optimization, BioShock Remastered sometimes suffers from performance issues, especially on PC, where some players have reported crashes, framerate drops, and stability issues. These issues, while not systematic, can spoil the experience and harm immersion. One might expect a remaster to correct these flaws, but unfortunately, they still persist for some users.

[b]Summary[/b]
[u]BioShock Remastered[/u] is an invitation to rediscover one of the greatest masterpieces of video games, with a brushstroke that brings the unique atmosphere of Rapture back to life. For new players, it’s a great opportunity to explore this shattered utopia, question Andrew Ryan’s radical ideals, and find yourself faced with troubling moral choices. For old fans, it’s a nostalgic return to a familiar place, with a few modern touches that make the experience more visually appealing, but without bringing anything truly new.

[i]90/100[/i]

There's nothing new in this game for you in 2020, but you can say the same about Dead Space, another classic that's held on a pedestal while living in a genre that has evolved and moved well past it. It is a relic you should experience at least once in your life if you have any sort of fondness for FPS RPG's, to understand where the genre has gone and why it evolved the way it did.

Bioshock is a master of its own setting. From environmental storytelling to telling a very quotable story through masterful voicework. It completes its own experience with a nice round bow tie, making using of everything it set up. From deception to revenge, the game questions your own agency within itself, urging you to look back and see the clues you looked past.

Yet, the real part that may keep you around is the RPG freedom the game provides. With limited slots, you're tasked to choose between what active and passive skills to keep equipped. From a melee caveman with a wrench, to a hacker, scavenger, a steampunk mage, a soldier with a killer arsenal or any mix in between, Gene Tonics let you define the parts of your playstyle you want strengthened, and what parts made easier for your convenience while plasmids give you active skills to define your playstyle with further. 

As said, if FPS RPG's are a particular fondness of yours, you owe yourself a playthrough of Bioshock. Just be wary of Bioshock 2, as it sacrifices the quality of the story for an improved combat system, and of Bioshock Infinite, as it hardly connects with the mechanics and themes that made Bioshock work.
Though I haven't wholly tested this comparison (I intend to, soon, with a replay of it), a game that might better work as a spiritual successor is 2017's PREY, offering a similarly streamlined story with a similar sort of exploration freedom and mechanics.

BioShock is one of the most atmospheric and thought-provoking games I’ve ever played. The world of Rapture is hauntingly beautiful, the story is gripping with unforgettable twists, and the gameplay blends action and strategy perfectly. Even years later, it holds up as a shining example of storytelling in gaming. An absolute must-play.

The actual game, beneath the remaster, is great. The improvements to HUD elements, physics and graphics are welcome, but as an overall remaster, this isn't exactly perfect.

Still recommend this overall, and if you don't want the remaster, you get the original game as well. I did personally suffer some crashes and annoying sound issues when I would switch/reload weapons, but I am unsure of if these were also in the original release. F8 is the quick save button, and I'd recommend using it a lot.

Ah, Bioshock. It's one of those games that has been sitting in my backlog for years collecting dust before I finally decided to start it up out of curiosity. Back during its 2007 release year, it was lauded for its artistic quality and themes, but as a gamer from 2021 revisiting a two-decade old game, how does it fare after a 10-hour long playtime?

Overall, it fares well. Bioshock 1 is one of those "masterpieces in its time, dated but decent in present day" games. It holds up similarly to games like Half Life 1 and Fallout 3: it has a surprising amount of variety for gunplay and customization, and has excellent strengths in its storytelling and style. However, expect to feel the age of the game and the clunkiness that accompanies an FPS of this time period.

The game's biggest strengths are its presentation and ambience. The game takes place in a dystopian retrofuturistic underwater city of Rapture, and you are thrown in without much context whatsoever. This cold open works well as it ends up being very intriguing. The backstory and lore are its absolute strongest points as it details the efforts of Rapture attempting to be the perfect society free from rules and regulations, which eventually causes conflicts and its own idealogies to fail. I've yet to play a game that has such a strong narrative focused on how society should be run and how it can be pushed to the extreme: it's like walking through a philosophical discussion.

The main plot, while acclaimed for its time, was not very interesting to me personally, as I've had the joy of playing Undertale, Danganronpa and Oneshot (though the initial twist did hit quite well). The core concept of harvesting or freeing Little Sisters are also not done as well as I'd like, as all it does is alter a few sets of dialogue and some cutscenes near the end of the game. You are also not punished severely for harvesting all Little Sisters, which means that the main deciding factor for harvesting them is the player's own moral compass.

Gameplay wise, it is decent and feels much like Half Life 1. You get an assortment of weaponry and different bullets that are more effective for different enemy types. You also get an impressive amount of plasmids (skills) that let you do things like shock enemies or summon bees, and can upgrade your abilities with additional addons for even more perks. Because of this, there's actually a lot of freedom to deal with enemies the way you want, which is impressive for a game of its age. The game even has ragdolls that you can whack and throw around, and that is always a major selling point for me. 

Outside of that though, this is where the datedness starts to be felt: fights tend to have clunky "old game difficulty". Movement is jittery, enemies instantly shoot you upon leaving cover, and you can burn out your resources (money) if you end up dying too often. As Bioshock was developed for a console, the default keybinds are also very dated: having C for crouch, Z for zoom, and mouse wheel to scroll through plasmids definitely feels like it's made by people from another era, though thankfully you can rebind those.

Hacking is a key part of the game but also not something I was very keen on doing, as while the puzzles are not that difficult, you're literally forced to sit down and solve a logic puzzle during an action game. In certain areas you have to get past security cameras or turrets: hacking them provides high utility as they become your bodyguards, but failing the minigame causes damage or calls an alarm that is bound to overwhelm you. This can make large fights very frustrating, as one wrong hack can mean you'll be even more screwed.

Finally, for those curious about bugs in this version, I did not encounter any game-breaking ones, but here are some significant ones I ran into:
-Screen tearing. (turn on Vsync, though it will cause the game to crash at first)
-Inventory hotkeys are buggy: your wrench and pistol may switch around, and your plasmid arrangement will go all over the place. (Not a game-breaking issue, but still an annoyance that you have to get used to. No fix apart from restarting an older save)
-Audio bugs: footsteps playing near dead enemies, and a battle theme looping endlessly during one encounter (switch maps to fix it)

All in all, a decent though dated experience. The setting is something I will fondly remember, though I hope the gameplay improves in the next two games. I recommend trying it when you can: don't expect too much from the plot twists, but stay for the premise.

Standing there, in his big suit with a drill the size of his own suit on his hand and the noise he makes... how eerily atmospheric it was coming across him. Then you have the Little Sisters, who, at first glance look all innocent and sweet until you see one with a needle harvesting Adam, but for some reason... you still want to protect them.

⚫The Plasmids. Incinerate!, which sets people on fire, sets oil ablaze and melts ice. Winter Blast, which freezes enemies solid with a cool effect and it puts out fires. Electro bolt, which electrocutes your enemies, opens up doors that need power and shocks water. These are the basic plasmids... but if you want more OOMF - HYPNOTIZE BIG DADDY. Yes, you read that right. 
⚫As of 25th November 2024 onward - there seems to be no more suttering, FPS drops, crashing e.t.c since they removed the 2K launcher. (for me anyway)

⚫AI a bit predictable. 
⚫Sometimes the gameplay loop gets a tad - repetitive. Run around, loot. Repeat.

Sorry, I got lost in the world of Rapture and Bioshock writing this review. BioShock™ Remastered is one of the greatest video-games of all time. A masterpiece. The Remaster only brings that "masterpiece" back to life for new and returning players. For me, I felt so nostalgic returning to this gorgeous, expertly written story!

What will you do? Explore Rapture? Save as many Little Sisters as you can? or will you crumble under the weight of the sea and be controlled by Andrew Ryan forever? The choice is yours. 

[h1][b] "A man chooses. A Slave obeys" [/b][/h1]

[h1]The gist of it:[/h1]
Replaying Bioshock reminded me of better times, and it's a shame that besides very few exceptions such as Prey, we never really received similar games, immersive sims more specifically. It's a dying breed, gamers these days prefer battle passes and garbage loot-focused online games. Gaming is no longer a passion for developers, it's just a way to make money off of dumb kids and adults by shoving gambling in them. But enough about that, Bioshock, is now considered a classic for many, a fantastic first-person shooter, with one of the best atmospheres ever made. 

👍 [u]The good parts:[/u]
+One of the best atmospheres ever made
+Great combat and its mechanics
+Well crafted story

👎[u]The bad parts:[/u]
-Hacking mini-games are boring and repetitive

[h1]Story[/h1]
Would you kindly play Bioshock? You start on a plane that crashes in the ocean near a dubious lighthouse. Upon entering you are transported to one of the best locations in gaming, Rapture, a city under the sea. As you bask in its beauty, you are immediately plunged into its chaos and horror with genetically modified humans, creepy girls, and so on and so forth. Everything feels overwhelming but exciting and beaming with mystery. A voice guides you through Rapture in hopes of helping him but the man behind the city, Andrew Ryan, won't allow it. 

The story is linear, you have almost no control over it, except for your choices in dealing with the little sisters. I won't spoil what's what, but it will impact the ending so think very carefully about your choices. There is no turning back. Andrew Ryan and Atlas are the meat of the story, they are constantly at war with one another and you are in the middle of it. Most of the story is told through radio interactions which was a good choice for the genre. 

Talking more would be spoiling but suffice it to say, there are a lot of interesting characters you'll meet as well as voice recordings that will enrich the story of Rapture. You do not need a million walls of text or nonstop dialogues or tons of cutscenes to tell a fantastic story. This is what modern developers have forgotten. Seems like these days, a protagonist that talks to himself/herself constantly is considered "amazing narration". What a load of crap. 

Story rating: 8.5/10

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As I reinstalled the game and started replaying it after so many years, I thought to myself, no way the combat will still feel good compared to Today's standards. I was wrong. It's better. It is insane that Bioshock does things I haven't seen done in modern games yet. It seems developers have stopped innovating and are just focused on money. 

Bioshock's shooting mechanics are just like any other shooter. All guns feel very impact'ish, especially the shotgun, they can be upgraded, and they also come with ammo variations such as ammo suited for armored targets. The other huge mechanics are the plasmids. You basically have these powers that can burn, shock, confuse enemies, and much more. The enemies react quite impressively, if you burn them, they will run for water and extinguish themselves. If you shock the water, everyone including yourself will get shocked. When was the last time we saw in a modern game an AI that would react accordingly? No one bothers with such small details anymore because the new generation of kid gamers are f'ing idiots. 

There's also a hacking mechanic which is pretty much the same puzzle for everything you hack. It's a mini-game where you have to control the flow of a liquid to its destination by placing the right tubes and avoiding alarms. If you fail, an alarm is sounded or you take damage. It gets pretty repetitive and boring really fast but luckily you can craft or find auto-hacking tools, as well as other things like ammo and whatnot. 

Gameplay rating: 8.5/10

[h1]Audio[/h1]
A story told mostly through voice recordings and radio has to obviously have at the very least good voice acting. Bioshock has fantastic voice acting, especially Andrew Ryan and Atlas, the main roles of the game. But that does not stop there, as all of the side characters also do a good job such as Cohen. 

The sound effects are pretty good, they sound a bit muffled, and lower quality but not that big of a deal. As for the soundtrack, it plays very rarely and only in key moments, but when it does, it fits perfectly well with the tone of the game. 

Audio rating: 8.5/10

[h1]Graphics, performance and tech analysis[/h1]
Bioshock is an immersive sim at heart. While its level design is not super complicated, it is still something I would prefer over open-world stuff. There are a lot of off-main paths to find, and lots of secrets to discover, and every corner of the game is beaming with incredible atmosphere and detail. The game still holds up well after so many years. 

Tech-wise, it blew everyone's minds when it was released, the water looked incredible, and still does, the colors, the textures, the AI, everything was top-notch. It had some issues, that are still found Today, such as crashes and lots of bugs but they are never really that annoying. 

Graphics, performance and tech analysis score: 9/10

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Would you kindly play Bioshock if you haven't? Would you kindly replay it again to see how much gaming has gone downhill? A phenomenal game, a classic that I will never forget. 

[h1]Final score: 8.6/10[/h1]

[h1]Detailed review without any major spoilers.[/h1]

The whole game takes place in Rapture - an underwater city. Don't expect to be in the water though. It's hard to follow the story mostly because of the sound quality, almost everything you hear is coming through a radio. There aren't many people you can interact with and by that I mean actual characters that matter. There are literally unlimited number of enemies though. They seem to spawn every now and then so you never feel like you're running around in an empty map.

Speaking of maps, every mission takes place in a huge location which thankfully is not that confusing because of the map which feels like DOOM RPG's map. There are a lot of audio diaries scattered throughout the game and if you're looking to follow the story, you should try to find and listen to every single one of them. If you're not interested in the story the game-play alone is worth the purchase.

Game-play is unique for a game of its time. You can carry various types of weapons in one hand and plasmids in the other. Plasmids are biologically shocking to say the least. There are so many things you can do with different plasmids. You can upgrade both your weapons and your plasmids. Upgrading weapons and plasmids not only changes their power but also changes their look and animation. There are also some passive abilities available which you can gather by collecting tonics. Tonics introduces a bit of RPG elements in the game. You can switch to your preferred play-style by choosing to use different kinds of tonics.

You can upgrade weapons at limited numbers of 'one-use' Power to the People machines which are well hidden or needs some puzzles to be solved in order to get access to. You can upgrade health, EVE and plasmids from Gatherer's Garden machines which are somewhat rare to find. You can purchase ammo at El Ammo Bandito machines which can be found in so many places. You can buy health / EVE / food / drinks at Circus of Values machine which can also be found at plenty of places. You can find ammo, health, EVE, money and foods / drinks throughout the map as well and by searching bodies of dead enemies. 

EVE is needed to use plasmids. Foods & drinks can increase your health and decrease your EVE or vice versa or increase both. You can swap your tonics (passive abilities) at a Gene Bank machine which are not available everywhere like the ammo or vending machine. But there's always one or two where you need them. This whole thing may seem confusing but it's actually quite addicting and not confusing at all once you get the hang of it.

Let's come to the story, there are two different endings, a good one and a bad one. The bad ending leaves things at a cliffhanger while the good ending makes most sense. It's also worth mentioning that the game BioShock Infinite assumes that you had picked the good ending - not the bad one. I found both endings to be a bit unsatisfying. The story, as I said before is hard to understand because of the audio quality and the horrible subtitle fonts don't help much. But if you do understand the dialogues and listen to audio diaries, then you'll find out what makes BioShock so great. The story is great. If you are not planning on playing BioShock 2 and Infinite, then the story is just good enough. There are some surprises that will blow your mind. I highly recommend focusing on the story.

Combat is awesome. You can create your unique character builds at Gene Bank machines - combine that with various weapons and plasmid combinations and you're in for a truly great experience. The Big Daddy encounters are way too easy on the easiest difficulty, so I'd suggest cranking up the difficulty a bit to have an even greater experience. You don't have to engage those brutes most of the time but they do provide great rewards and are a big part of the game. Using a Gatherer's Garden machine requires ADAM as currencies and you'll need to engage those big daddies in order to get to the girl he was protecting - the girl has ADAM, how you choose to take it from her though, is up to you and this will affect which ending you're gonna get. Even though there are several enemy types, it does get boring in the long run and they all look kinda same. There are machines which you can hack to get more benefits or make it your own (drones, turrets & security cameras).

Not much left to say except, it's a good game and does an amazing job at visual storytelling. If you're not interested in the story or finding it confusing to follow, get it for the game-play mechanic. If you're not interested in the game-play or finding it confusing, get it for the story. Would you kindly look past some minor flaws and save often?

Step 1: Disabled steam overlay and use desktop game theatre.... by right clicking game in library and selecting properties. 

Step 2: right click game in steam library again and select Local Files and click browse local files. Find Bioshock.exe right click it and select properties. Under the compatibility tab click run as administrator (it will now have a tick next to it), also select windows 8 in run in compatibility mode for and click apply. Do the same thing in change settings for all users. Next select the security tab and ensure all users have full control setting enabled. click apply.

Step 3: For pc's with more than 4 cpu cores. Run the game. once its started click ctrl+alt+delete at the same time and select task manager. click the details tab. right click bioshockhd.exe and click on set affinity. disable cores 1,3,5,7. On a quad core disabling cores 1 and 3 may help.

This game, however, is a masterpiece of storytelling and setting, and if you've never played Bioshock before, then you're missing out on one of the finest crafted games of all time.  

Compared to many other video games, where the story is told directly to the player, this game tells its story through audiotapes and setting.  As you explore the underwater megalopolis of Rapture, you see what kind of city it was before the rapid and tragic decline of behavior and descent into chaos for Rapture's denizens.  The audiotapes tell individual stories of various people and help to paint the picture of what led to the destruction of Rapture's society.

Gameplay wise, the action is hit or miss.  Hacking and upgrading your character's plasmids and tonics are fun, but the gun play leaves something to be desired.  For example, you can't have your plasmids in one hand and your gun in the other -- you have to switch between them.  In gun fights, it's a bit janky, and not particularly smooth.  Bioshock 2 fixes this problem, however.

Overall, I'd pick this game up when it's on sale.  For $20, the game is far too old to justify that price.  While the game is beautiful in some parts, the graphics do look a bit dated.
